cells.tense: The pen is in your hand now, and the clearing has already opened under you.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Find the part of what you've been tending that's finished — done, gathered, over — and stop carrying that part. Give the hours to what hasn't grown yet.
cells.core: A built thing came down and you're in the open part of it, seeing what was false as a mercy. People usually brace under a clearing; your hands stay steady because you've learned growth from watching it happen — when to water, when to leave alone. That's what keeps this page clean instead of frightening. There's an itch, when something opens, to start the next frame fast so the open ground doesn't have to be sat in. You don't have to. Nothing needs rebuilding today. What's finished and already gathered can be finished. What's still sprouting is where your hands are needed, and the work there is the whole of it. Stay in the clearing as someone who grows things, not as someone who owes it a new structure.
cells.sheetLine: You can tend what's growing without rebuilding the frame.
cells.verb: tending something in its early growth, learning by hand how it takes
cells.place: in the clearing where a structure that couldn't hold just came down

cells.tense: You will have the next trellis half-built before the clearing has finished opening.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Picture how the next thing might go, and let one detail land that you didn't plan. Then close the sketch.
cells.core: A wall came down and your first move is scaffolding something new before the dust settles. Care running ahead of itself. You see what might grow and you start building for it in the same breath, and the imagined version gets solid enough to stand on before the real ground has been looked at. In a clearing, speed can look like repair. Picture one step out and close the sketch there. Slow hands grow things at least as well as fast ones — the pace is the only thing changing. The patch you keep drawing isn't a warning. It's a picture, and it's allowed to stay a picture while the open ground stays open.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the doorway of a clearing that opened in the past.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin one thing this week for no useful reason — a page to sketch, a route to walk — and start it only because starting is what you like.
cells.core: A structure came down and you're at the edge of the open patch like it belongs to someone else. Your hands know the work — tend, water, watch — and they aren't reaching. Skill and care are present, and the appetite for beginning is what's quiet: the spark that used to come with simply starting, before you knew whether it would take. Everything that's ever grown under your hands started as something small and unfigured, and you were the one who put it in the ground. Nothing about that has changed. The clearing doesn't move, and you don't either, until something gets planted. One cutting in soil, badly done if it comes out badly. First move is small, and it's yours.

cells.tense: You keep the garden alive in the open and file it under good conditions.
cells.act: govern by knowing what to surrender
cells.ask: When something in your care is finished, let it stay finished. Don't nurse it back or replant it, and notice whose call that was.
cells.core: Somebody has kept the garden alive since the frame came down. Things that were thin got tended until they held. The story you carry has the season friendly and the plants having good bones, and none of the work counted as a decision. It was. The clearing made room; hands kept it going. The older form of the same skill is knowing when a thing is finished instead of nursing it longer, and that call sits in you — it hasn't gone anywhere. Let one done thing be done. Keep that up for a few days before you mention it to anyone. The hands that did the work are the hands you have.
cells.sheetLine: The garden held because you kept it through the open.
